questiontext.text: In a singly-linked-list stack, at which end are push and pop performed?

answer.text: At the head of the list

feedback.text: Correct — inserting and removing at the head is O(1).

answer.text: At the tail of the list

feedback.text: Reaching the tail of a singly linked list would cost O(n) without a tail pointer.

answer.text: In the middle of the list

feedback.text: Stacks only touch one end, and finding the middle is not O(1).

answer.text: At a randomly chosen node

feedback.text: Stack access is not random.

generalfeedback.text: Operating at the head lets both push and pop stay O(1) with just a head pointer.

questiontext.text: What is the time complexity of push and pop at the head of a linked-list stack?

feedback.text: Correct — only the head pointer is rewired.

answer.text: O(n)

feedback.text: No traversal is needed to reach the head.

answer.text: O(log n)

feedback.text: There is no logarithmic search here.

answer.text: O(n log n)

feedback.text: That is unrelated to head insertion.

generalfeedback.text: Prepending a node and detaching the head are both constant-time pointer updates.

questiontext.text: What is a key advantage of a linked-list stack over a fixed-capacity array stack?

answer.text: It grows dynamically with no fixed capacity limit

feedback.text: Correct — nodes are allocated on demand, so it never overflows from a preset size.

answer.text: It provides O(1) random access by index

feedback.text: A linked list has no random access.

answer.text: It uses less memory per element

feedback.text: Each node adds a pointer, so it uses more, not less.

answer.text: It guarantees better cache locality

feedback.text: Scattered nodes generally hurt cache locality.

generalfeedback.text: The linked stack trades a per-node pointer and worse locality for unbounded, dynamic growth.

questiontext.text: What does a single node in a singly-linked-list stack contain?

answer.text: The data plus a next pointer to the following node

feedback.text: Correct — data and a single forward link.

answer.text: The data plus both a prev and a next pointer

feedback.text: That is a doubly linked node, not singly linked.

answer.text: Only the data, with no pointer

feedback.text: Without a link the nodes could not be chained.

answer.text: The data plus a numeric array index

feedback.text: Linked nodes chain by pointer, not by index.

generalfeedback.text: A singly linked node stores its payload and one next pointer.

questiontext.text: Which statements about a singly-linked-list stack are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: It follows LIFO order

feedback.text: Yes — it is still a stack.

answer.text: push and pop at the head are O(1)

feedback.text: Yes — just a head-pointer rewiring.

answer.text: It supports O(1) random access by index

feedback.text: No — a linked list has no random access.

answer.text: It has a fixed maximum capacity set at creation

feedback.text: No — it grows dynamically as nodes are allocated.

generalfeedback.text: A linked stack is LIFO with O(1) head operations, no random access, and no fixed capacity.

questiontext.text: A linked-list stack can grow dynamically without a fixed capacity.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — nodes are allocated on demand.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: It does grow dynamically; only array stacks have a fixed size.

questiontext.text: A singly-linked-list stack supports O(1) random access to any element by index.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Reaching an arbitrary node requires O(n) traversal from the head.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Correct — linked lists have no O(1) random access.

questiontext.text: In a linked-list stack, both push and pop occur at the ______ of the list.

answer.text: head

feedback.text: Correct — the head gives O(1) push and pop.

answer.text: head*

feedback.text: Correct — the head gives O(1) push and pop.
